Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00606
Third, necessary features do not stand apart from the thing that causes them. In any account, they depend on the cause of the thing itself.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00607

There is another problem: rest lasts for a stretch of time and can be divided along with that time. Any amount of rest between two motions could be shorter. What sets its length? The body's size, density, lightness, weight, and other features may set it.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00608

Those who deny rest also point to a large stone falling while a tiny seed is thrown upward in its path. If the seed must stop when it touches the stone, then the falling stone should stop too. The usual reply is that the seed turns back when the wind of the falling stone strikes it, so it stops before the two touch. But we can see cases where they touch while the smaller thing is still rising, as with an arrow going up or a hand rising against a heavy stone that is falling. They answer that it is unlikely, but not impossible, for the falling stone to stop.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00609

Al-Rāzī says that although this is far-fetched, it is possible, and the proof requires us to accept it. I ask what proof requires it. The proof requires real rest between two different motions, not a motion that is only called motion in a loose sense. A person sitting in a moving boat is at rest in themselves while moving only because of the boat. The first motion has already ended in rest. There is no impossibility in a body resting for part of the time while it remains in contact with something carrying it along, even if, left to itself, it would move in its natural direction because the outside force remains with it after the motion.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00610
X. How Motion Is Divided by What Causes It
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00611

Now that we have discussed motion's features, we can discuss its kinds. Motion that a thing undergoes in itself comes in three kinds: natural movement, movement by choice, and movement caused by something outside it. Taken more broadly, motion has four kinds: those three, plus motion that belongs to a thing only because it is joined to something else. We should not leave this fourth kind out of the other three, because it is still connected to one of them.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00612

Anything described as moving either moves in itself or moves only because it is joined to something moving. The second kind is movement a thing shares because it is carried along. For the first kind, the cause of motion is either within the thing or outside it. If it is outside, the motion is forced. If the cause is within, the thing either has awareness or it does not. If it does, the motion comes from the soul; if not, it is natural. Some motions are hard to place in this scheme, especially the pulse. People disagree about whether it is natural or chosen. In either case, is it movement from place to place, a change of position, or a change in size? Each view has its arguments in the medical books, especially in commentaries on the general parts of The Canon of Medicine.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00613

Some say that breathing is chosen in one respect and natural in another. A person can choose when to take a breath and can delay it, but still needs to breathe. This is what Avicenna means when he says breathing is voluntary and can be changed from its natural pattern. The objection that a sleeping person has no will and therefore should not breathe is mistaken. A sleeping person can make chosen movements without knowing or remembering that they are doing so. Growth is clearly natural: the nature of a growing thing makes it increase as food enters and spreads through it. According to careful doctors, the pulse is also not chosen and is not caused by an outside force. It comes from the vital power in the heart. Most people think it is movement from place to place; others say it is a change of position, and others a change in size.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00614

If someone says that natural motion can go only in one direction, either up or down, we reply that this is true only of the simple elements. In plants and animals, natural powers can produce motions in different directions and toward different ends. The heart and arteries expand outward from the center and then contract inward again. The aim of expansion is not to reach the outside, and the aim of contraction is not to reach the center. Their purpose is to drive out harmful air. The body needs both actions in turn, moment by moment, so one power can produce opposite effects at different times.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00615

I say it is better to divide motion into five kinds. There is another kind that may be called “directed by the soul.” The soul begins it by using the body's nature directly, without a separate act of choice. We can either divide natural motion into what happens through this use and what happens by nature on its own, or divide motion from the soul into what follows a separate choice and what happens through the soul's use of nature. The circular motion of the heavens is an example of this second kind: the soul uses nature to produce it.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00616

Ancient philosophers often said the heavens have a fifth kind of nature. Later thinkers could not fully explain what they meant, so they offered two readings. The first is that the movements of the heavens are not natural, but they do not oppose the nature of those bodies either. Their source is not something foreign to the bodies, so it is like nature. The second is that every power moves through an inward tendency. The first mover continually creates a new tendency in the body. This tendency may be called a nature because it is not a soul, a separate choice, or an outside force; it cannot stop moving or move in another direction, and it does not oppose the body's nature. If you use “nature” in this sense, you can say that the heavens move by nature. Ptolemy says that if someone chooses what is best and follows through, there is no difference between that and natural motion.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00617

I say, as I have already hinted, that the motions of the heavens are natural. They have changing natures that directly produce circular motion, and these natures are not separate from the souls and intelligences of the heavens. A fuller discussion belongs elsewhere.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00618
XI. What Does Natural Motion Seek?
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00619

Any natural state can be lost through forced change. A state may also be something nature has only as a possibility at one time and has fully brought about at another. Nature can move a thing toward such a state. When the outside force is removed, the thing returns to its natural state. And when a possibility becomes actual, the thing gains the completion that belongs to it.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00620

But there is a problem with motion from place to place. When a heavy body falls back down after being thrown upward, is it trying to reach the very center of the world? And do light bodies seek the outer edge of the heavens? That cannot be right. The earth as a whole cannot reach the center, and only the outer surface of fire can touch the inner surface of the outermost sphere. Yet the natural goal of a motion cannot be something impossible to reach. Also, if falling water sought the exact center, it would never float. If air sought the outer edge, it would not remain below fire.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00621

We cannot say that light bodies seek the outer edge but fire wins because it is stronger and gets there first. If that were so, when we place our hands over air, we would feel it pushing upward, just as we do when it is trapped in a vessel under water. Nor can each element simply seek a place in general, or some part of place in general. Places do not differ in themselves. And if a stone simply sought to be near the whole earth, then a stone dropped into a well should cling to the rim.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00622

Since these answers do not work, the right view is that nature seeks a region, but only when it has the right order among the regions. Water belongs above the earth and below the air: its coldness fits the earth, while its moistness and fluidity fit the air. The other elements fit their regions in the same way. If their natural regions were not arranged in this order, the elements would be ruined by being next to their opposites. Direction itself is not what nature seeks; it matters only when this proper order is present. Nature aims for this state and moves away from its opposite.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00623

We can see that a place may be natural even when the order around it is not. For example, air trapped in a porous brick that is hanging in the air draws water up from below. The air is trying to escape an unfamiliar boundary, so water rises through the brick's pores to take its place. This happens because there can be no empty space.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00624

Someone may ask whether this motion happens because a thing flees what is unnatural or because it seeks what is natural. We can say that both are involved; there is no conflict between them. It cannot be only a matter of fleeing the unnatural. If it were, motion could go in any direction, since no direction would be preferred. That is clearly false.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00625
XII. Can One Body Have Different Sources of Motion?
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00626

As for celestial bodies, after their essential motion they can have only circular motion in position and changes in the soul's qualities. They cannot change place or size, grow or shrink, become more or less dense, or undergo other changes such as heating, cooling, changing color or taste, or giving off a smell. As we shall see, they are free of these qualities. So they cannot have sources of these changes; otherwise nature would be idle, which is impossible.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00627

Bodies that come to be, especially those made of several elements, can have some of these qualities together, and can undergo the motions they bring about. One body may therefore contain sources of different motions. But it cannot contain both a source of straight motion and a source of circular motion. If it left its natural region, it would naturally move in a straight line toward its goal and also naturally turn in a circle away from that goal. That is impossible. Someone might reply that its circular tendency appears only while it is in its natural region. But then that tendency would not be built into its nature.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00628

Nor can circular motion be assigned to the soul. In our view, the soul acts only through nature. Also, we have established that a body can receive motion from an outside mover only if, by its nature, it already has a tendency of its own. Someone might object: does not nature cause motion when a body is outside its natural region, and rest when it is in that region? So why could it not cause a straight tendency when the body is out of place and a circular one when it is in place?
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00629

We reply that nature causes just one thing here: rest in the natural region. That rest may require motion to reach it. In short, nature can bring about rest only by bringing the body into that region. It does not need to give it a circular tendency, since all parts of place are alike.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00630
XIII. What Causes Forced Motion?
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00631

The soundest view is that forced motion comes from the nature within the body being forced. The outside force changes that nature and prepares it to produce the motion. Avicenna seems to say that the cause is a tendency given to the body by an outside mover. But pushing alone cannot explain forced motion. The push given by the outside mover does not last. If the body's nature gradually produces the motion, then nature is the cause after all.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00632

Nature can produce an unsuitable, forced tendency just as it can produce a suitable, natural one. This is like an illness or a foreign heat that the body's nature produces when it has been driven from its proper course. Once the body recovers, nature gives it what suits it again. Or consider a jagged shape: the nature of earth gives it this shape when force has pushed it away from the rounded shape it tends toward. It does not return to roundness because its natural dryness preserves its shape. As has been explained elsewhere, there is no contradiction here.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00633

Avicenna says that, without the repeated impacts of the air, which weaken the tendency, a body thrown upward would not return until it struck the inner surface of the heavens. But there is a problem with his account. How can impacts from the air fail to weaken the body's natural tendency until that tendency becomes stronger again, while still weakening the forced tendency? One possible answer is that the impacts have this effect only while the body is outside its natural region. As it moves farther and farther away, they weaken its forced tendency until that power is spent and its original power takes over.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00634

Still, this issue cannot be fully resolved without returning to one of our Eastern principles. The principle says that when an outside force acts on a body, the body's form changes in its very substance and essence. For example, molten iron has a form that heats it, alongside its iron form. A stone thrown upward has a form that makes it light, alongside its stony form. Several essential features that appear separately in different beings can come together in the existence of one form. This principle answers the objection that the power moving a stone upward is the form of fire, and so, if it were in the stone, it would be an accident within a substance, even though it was itself a substance before.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00635

There are four possible views about the cause of forced motion. The cause is either inside the body being moved or outside it. If it is inside, it either remains until the motion ends or it does not. If it does not remain, this is the view that one motion produces another, and so on. If it remains, this is the view that the outside force gives the body a power by which it continues to move.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00636

If the cause is outside the body, it must be another body. It may move the body by pushing or pulling. The pushing view says that the air ahead of the thrown object bends back and pushes it. The pulling view says that the mover pushes both the air and the object, but the air is lighter and moves faster, pulling the object along with it.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00637

These last two views fail. If the pulling or pushing does not last until the motion ends, we need another cause for the motion, and the same question comes up again. If it does last, we still have to ask what causes that pulling or pushing. The view that one motion produces another also fails: it would mean an effect exists after its cause is gone, and that a cause acts when it is no longer there.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00638

Once these weak views are set aside, only one sound view remains, though it needs careful examination. Forced motion can occur in place. It may go against a body's nature completely, as when a stone is thrown upward, or only partly, as when a stone is dragged across the ground. Carrying a body is closer to motion that happens incidentally. Forced change in position, such as turning a body around, combines pulling and pushing.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00639

It can also result from two motions working against each other. This happens, for example, in molten metal. A part lifted by boiling rises, then falls again by nature. As it nears its resting place, its natural downward tendency grows stronger. Once this tendency appears, it resists the heat and moves downward. It shifts its resting place by the same amount that it had been raised, and so it turns in a circle between the high point and the new resting place. The turning is not around the resting place itself.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00640

A body may tumble because of two outside causes, or because its natural tendency works together with a push or a pull, as when a ball rolls down a hill. Forced change in size includes swelling and the loosening of water in a bottle when the air is sucked out. Forced shrinking includes wasting away through illness, though not shrinking with age: from the point of view of the whole living thing, that is natural; from the point of view of the individual body, it is forced.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00641

Forced change in quality includes water being heated, illnesses that change a body's condition, and changes in the soul's habits. Ignorance may grow, unbelief deepen, or greed and other faults become stronger over time. These go against the natural state of human beings. Since we hold that things come into being through changes in their very substance, this kind of change may also be natural or forced. Natural examples include an embryo developing from semen and a plant growing from a seed. Forced examples include making fire by striking stones, or the work of alchemists who turn copper into gold and tin into silver. Decay may also be natural, as when an old animal dies or trees dry out over time, or forced, as when death is caused by murder or poison, or a tree is cut down.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00642
XIV. Why Every Body Has a Tendency to Move in a Straight Line or a Circle
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00643

Every body, simply as a body, can move from one place to another or turn from one position to another. This is because it either has a source of that motion within it, or it does not. If it does, that is clear. If it does not, then it must be easier to move it from outside. The stronger a body’s tendency in one direction, the harder it is to move it the other way. A thing with an obstacle in its way is harder to move than when nothing stands in its way.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00644

So, if we imagine a body with no tendency at all, it would be as easy as possible to move from outside. It would then have to move from place to place all at once, with no time passing. But motion without time is impossible. Therefore, no body can exist without some natural tendency to move. That is enough for a reader considering the argument carefully, even if it may not convince someone looking for every possible objection.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00645

We can make the argument clearer. A bodily power can be greater or smaller, finite or unlimited, only because of the numbers, sizes, or durations connected with it. It must be limited in number, duration, and strength: the number of its effects and motions must be finite, and so must the time they last, whether we look at time increasing or decreasing. A motion takes time, and any amount can be considered finite or unlimited. The same is true of differences in duration and number, or differences in strength.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00646

Here is what this means. Powers are connected to things that have size or number. For example, a power may produce one continuous action over time, or a series of actions that can be counted. We can ask whether the action has a limit or not. This may be based on the amount of work done or on how many actions occur. For amount of work, we can ask about one unified action over a period of time, or about a continuing action without treating its parts as one or many. In this way, powers fall into three kinds.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00647

The first kind produces one action over different lengths of time. Imagine archers whose arrows all travel the same distance, but in different times. The archer whose arrow takes less time is stronger. If the strength were unlimited, the arrow would cover the distance in no time.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00648

The second kind produces some action continuously for different lengths of time. Imagine archers whose arrows stay in the air for different amounts of time. The one whose arrow stays in the air longer is stronger. If the effect continued without limit, it would do so for an unlimited time.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00649

The third kind produces repeated actions that differ in number. Imagine archers who shoot different numbers of arrows. The one who shoots more has greater power. If the effect had no limit, the number of actions would be unlimited. The first kind differs in strength, the second in duration, and the third in number. Since an unlimited strength would mean an effect occurs in no time at all, it is plainly impossible: motion can happen only over time that can be divided.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00650

Forced motion also changes according to the body moved. The larger the body, the more it resists, because its nature is stronger. A small body resists less. So an outside force moves a larger body less easily.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00651

Every motion involves three things that vary together: time, distance, and degree of speed or slowness. If two motions agree in two of these, they must agree in the third. If they agree in one and differ in another by a certain ratio, they must differ by that ratio in the third as well.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00652

Suppose an outside force moves a body with no natural tendency through a given distance. Its motion must take some particular amount of time, since there is no motion except in a particular case, with a particular duration. Now suppose that the same force moves another body with a natural tendency through the same distance. It must take longer, because the body's own tendency resists the forced motion. Otherwise, motion with an obstacle would be no different from motion without one.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00653

Now suppose the same force moves a third body that has a natural tendency. Let the strength of that tendency compared with the first body's tendency match the ratio between the first two times. Suppose the body with no tendency takes one tenth as long as the body with the first tendency. If the ratios hold, the body with no tendency and the third body must take the same time. The third body's tendency would then have no effect, as if it did not exist. That is impossible.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00654

Several objections have been raised. First, someone may reject the possibility of a tendency whose strength has the exact ratio to another tendency that the two times or distances have. Perhaps weakness reaches a limit, with nothing weaker beyond it. Second, someone may deny that a natural tendency resists a forced one, even if it has the ratio described. Resistance, they may say, occurs only above a certain strength.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00655
Third, the times are measured quantities, while the levels of resistance are counted. The two may not match; the time ratio might even be irrational.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00656

We answer all three objections this way: degrees of strength and weakness in bodily powers and qualities have no natural stopping point in either direction, just as amounts can increase or decrease without reaching a final limit. A body's size cannot be divided down to a smallest possible piece, nor increased to a largest possible size, unless some outside limit stops it. Tendencies and forces are the same. Even the weakest tendency resists something, since existence is always a source of effect. Its resistance may simply be too slight to notice. The same is true of qualities connected to quantity: they can be equal or different, greater or smaller, countable, measurable together, or impossible to measure by a common unit. They differ from quantity itself because they depend on it.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00657

The strongest objection is this: either motion can exist without resistance for some amount of time, or it cannot. If it can, then part of the time taken by motion with strong resistance is for the motion itself, and the rest is for the resistance. If it cannot, the argument fails because it assumes something impossible: motion without resistance. Perhaps, then, the body's lack of a natural tendency is not the cause of the problem.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00658

I reply that we can choose the second answer. That does not defeat the proof. The proof shows that if motion without resistance took some time, the three bodies described above would lead to the impossible result that two motions take the same time even though one meets resistance and the other does not. So motion without resistance cannot take time. But every motion must take time. It is therefore impossible for a body with no natural tendency to move at all. We may also choose the first answer. Admitting that an imagined motion without speed or slowness would take time does not mean that any real motion has a separate time for motion itself and another for its speed, slowness, or resistance.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00659

The argument can then be stated this way: if a body with no natural tendency moved, it would take time. Otherwise, a condition would fail to follow from what it entails. But if it took time, its duration would have to match that of a body with a tendency, which is impossible. So it would take no time, which is also impossible. Therefore a body with no natural tendency cannot move at all. This objection was made in another form by several later thinkers, including Abū al-Barakāt. Al-Rāzī followed him. They say motion itself calls for one amount of time, and resistance calls for another. A body facing resistance has both, while a body without resistance has only the first. The time taken by motion itself would therefore stay the same in every case; only the time caused by resistance would vary. The total time would vary once the two were added. This, they say, avoids the contradiction.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00660

Al-Tusi's reply to this objection also answers most of the later objections. If the claim that motion itself calls for time means that motion, apart from any degree of speed or slowness, calls for time, that is plainly false. Motion cannot be separated from speed and slowness. Nothing inseparable from something else can call for a separate feature without that other thing, even if the other thing is not itself what brings the feature about. If instead the claim means that motion, with no particular degree of speed or slowness in mind, calls for some amount of time, that is also mistaken. Motion as such is related to degrees of speed and slowness as a general kind is related to its particular kinds: it cannot exist without one of them.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00661

The careful scholar al-Tusi sets out a starting point in his commentary on The Pointers: if motion comes from the soul, the soul can set the speed or slowness it imagines as fitting. The soul then produces a tendency in keeping with that choice, and motion follows. But motion that does not come from the soul—motion caused by nature or by an outside force—needs something else to set its speed or slowness, since nature is not aware of what it is doing. By its own nature, it would move without time, or as fast as possible. Since that cannot happen, something must set its tendency and its degree of movement. This can happen only when the mover meets resistance in what it moves. Nature by itself does not vary. An outside force, if taken at its strongest, does not vary either. But tendency does vary. So the difference between faster and slower motion comes from another factor, called resistance.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00662

That resistance may come from outside the body being moved, as when the medium is more or less dense. Or it may come from within the body. It cannot come from within during natural motion, since a thing's own nature cannot both require an action and resist that same action. But it does resist forced motion: the natural tendency or the soul's tendency is opposed to the forced tendency. So if both outside and inside resistance were absent, there would be no difference between speed and slowness, and there would be no motion. This is why philosophers have argued from these two kinds of motion, at different times, that there can be no empty space and that bodies must have a natural tendency to move. Al-Tusi then answers the objection in two ways.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00663

First, motion cannot have one amount of time for itself and another because of its speed or slowness. As we have shown, motion can exist only at some degree of speed or slowness. A motion that has no such degree does not exist, so it cannot call for time. Second, motion itself cannot call for time. If it existed without any degree of speed or slowness, then a second motion taking half as long—or twice as long—would be faster or slower than it. Yet we supposed that the first motion had no degree of speed or slowness. That is a contradiction.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00664

Some later writers object that al-Tusi has narrowed the proof to natural and forced motion, and that many of his claims are open to challenge. He says that motion cannot exist without one of the two forms of resistance, without noticing, they say, that this is what the proof is meant to establish. They also object to his claim that the outside force does not vary. If he means the force used in the three examples has no difference between them, then the critic agrees: if the force set the speed, the motion would not vary. That is precisely the critic's view: when resistance is set aside, forced motion itself calls for a certain time and degree of speed, and the times then increase according to the amount of resistance. But if al-Tusi means that all outside forces are the same in every case, then forced motions could never vary in speed, which is plainly false.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00665

The same applies to his claim that the body receiving motion does not vary. The body in the examples is supposed to be the same. The critic also denies that another factor must resist the mover. That factor, the critic says, could simply be the body's natural tendency. In his commentary on The Pointers, al-Tusi clearly says that every motion has some degree of speed or slowness. This is a quality that can grow stronger or weaker, and the difference depends on what the motion is compared with. Because motion cannot be separated from this quality, and nature cannot itself grow stronger or weaker, nature alone cannot set the degree of a particular motion. It must first produce something that can grow stronger or weaker as the body changes in size, density, looseness, position, or some other way. That is the tendency. Al-Tusi's account plainly treats tendency as what sets the speed or slowness of motion.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00666

Even if we grant that, one fixed tendency added to nature or to an outside force cannot set one particular degree of motion. The same force and tendency can produce different speeds. A stone with the same tendency can move at different speeds depending on how dense the medium is. The denser the medium, the slower the motion; the thinner it is, the faster. If the medium had no density at all, as in empty space, the motion would take no time. That is impossible, so the medium must have some density and there can be no empty space.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00667

Al-Tusi's answer to the critic's other objections is as follows. Why could the factor setting speed not be something besides resistance from inside or outside, such as a magnet pulling on iron? We reply that we can imagine a body moving with none of the outside factors the critic names, apart from what is already part of motion. And why, the critic asks, can something inside the body not resist its natural motion? Because a thing's own nature cannot both require a motion and resist that same motion. We reply that this objection would work only if the same inner cause were doing both things. But there can be two different causes within: one may produce a motion while the other resists it. A bird, for example, may fall under its own weight while its soul makes it fly upward. So the argument cannot prove that empty space is impossible by looking at natural motion alone.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00668

The critic then grants this point, but says one form of resistance is enough to set the speed. If so, we cannot use forced motion to prove there is no outside resistance, such as a medium; resistance from within would already be enough. In the same way, he says, we cannot use forced motion to prove there is an inner tendency, since resistance from the medium would already set the speed. So, he concludes, neither natural nor forced motion can prove the claims philosophers draw from them.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00669

I say these objections all fail. The earlier argument already answered the claim that motion without resistance is impossible. Nor does Al-Tusi rule out the soul's choosing a degree of speed or slowness for motion from the soul. As for the objection about the outside force, it comes from misunderstanding him. He is making a general point: since motion can vary in speed and slowness, its immediate cause must itself have some variation, so that each degree of cause brings about a matching degree of motion. But neither nature nor an outside force, considered by itself, varies in this way. His point is like the familiar view that a substance does not become more or less of itself. In our view, nature does change and vary in itself, and all differences ultimately return to it. I will explain this at greater length elsewhere.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00670

The critic also says that perhaps the body's natural tendency, rather than some resistance, sets the speed. Al-Tusi's best reply is this: a tendency can be stronger or weaker. It is a felt quality, and for him it lies between nature and motion. Nature remains stable; motion changes. The tendency connects the two. It is a real quality that can be stronger or weaker, and it comes about through outside causes.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00671

The critic then asks why there cannot be another cause that sets the degree of motion, such as a magnetic force. We reply that we can imagine the moving body without any of the outside causes the critic has named, except those that are part of the motion itself. The critic also says that the same resistance can allow many degrees of speed, so it cannot determine which one occurs. But this is the same problem as before: with one inner or outside resistance, how can the three motions in the proof have different speeds? The critic's argument against empty space would fail in the same way if we let inner resistance set the speed while ruling out outside resistance.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00672

Nor can the critic show that natural motion has no inner resistance by saying that one thing cannot both require an action and resist it. The explanation given above already answers this: two different inner causes may be at work. A bird may fall by its own weight while its soul makes it fly to a perch. The soul is outside the elemental nature of the body, just as magnetic force is outside it. So the bird is no counterexample. Even if we accept the critic's point, one type of resistance would be enough to set the degree of motion. In that case, we could not use forced motion to prove that the medium is not empty, since a body's inner tendency would set the speed. And we could not use forced motion to prove an inner tendency exists, since the medium could set it.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00673

We can answer this by returning to the point already made: every forced action on a body, and every body's ability to receive such an action, depends on its nature. The force is always a bodily power that acts by pulling, pushing, heating, cooling, or otherwise preparing the body. A body can be affected by these actions only if it already has a nature. Matter itself cannot receive them until it has become a particular kind of thing. We will return to this in the discussion of specific forms.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00674

A further point: you have heard me say many times that the immediate, direct cause of every motion is always nature. That holds whether the motion comes from the soul, an outside force, or nature. So there is no need to spend more time proving that forced motion has an inner resistance. Also, philosophers have proved that every body has a substantial form. This form makes it the kind of body it is, completes its matter, begins its effects, and gives it the features stated in its definition. Here, they want to prove that this form exists as the source that shapes and limits motion and tendency. It is called “nature” in this role, just as it is called “form,” “power,” or “completion” in other roles.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00675
XV. Bodily Forces Have Limits in How They Move Things
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00676

We have already seen that a power is finite or unlimited only because of its relation to the size or number of things in which it exists or on which it acts. If bodies were unlimited in size or number, the powers within them would be unlimited in those respects, because a power is divided along with the body it exists in. The second case concerns what the power can affect. If that had no limit, the power would have no limit either. As you have seen, this can be understood in three ways: strength, number, or duration. We shall now show that a bodily force cannot be unlimited in strength. The motion it produces would either take time or happen without time. The first is impossible, because time can be divided: there could always be a shorter time, so the motion would not be infinitely fast. The second is also impossible. Motion is the covering of a distance, and every distance can be divided; a part of it is covered before the whole. For this reason, even a separate power that acts with unlimited strength cannot directly move a body.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00677

A bodily force also cannot produce unlimited effects in number or duration. Such a force is either natural or forced. If it is natural, the larger body should be at least as able to receive motion as the smaller one. If they differed, the difference would not come from their bodily nature, which they share; it could not come from a natural cause without making the motion unnatural; and it could not come from forced resistance, which we have set aside. Yet the larger and smaller bodies do differ in how they receive motion. So the difference must come from the strength of the power: the force in the larger body is greater, because it is spread through the whole body, while the force in the smaller body is only a part of it.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00678

In forced motion, the same force moves a large body less than a small one, because the larger body offers more resistance. With this in place, we can see that no natural bodily force can move its body without limit. The force within the whole body is greater than the force within any part of it. If both the whole and the part were moved without limit from the same starting point, the effect of the part would equal the effect of the whole, which is impossible. If the smaller body were moved only a finite amount, then the extra amount moved by the whole would be in a finite ratio to it: the ratio between the part and the whole. So the movement of the whole would also be finite. The same reasoning applies to forced motion, though there the larger body reaches its limit first.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00679
Several objections have been raised. First, the argument assumes that everything in a body is divided when the body is divided. But this is not true of unity, existence, a point, or relations.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00680

I reply that, as we have explained, unity and existence are one and the same in each thing. They are features of what a thing is when we analyze it in thought. The existence of a body is divided along with the body, and its unity is the continuity that holds it together, as we have already explained. As for a point or a relation, neither is simply a feature of a thing because it is divided. Each belongs to a thing along with some further feature—for example, a point marks an end. If a relation belonged to the divided thing just as divided, then the relation itself would also be divided, as happens with equality and alignment.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00681

A second objection says there is no necessary ratio between the effect of a part of a force and the effect of the whole. If ten people lift and carry something a certain distance in a certain time, it does not follow that one of them could carry it one tenth of that distance, or carry it the same distance in ten times as long. One person might not move it at all. A small piece of fire might not burn a piece of stone, either.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00682

I reply that there is no such thing as an existing force with no effect unless something outside it prevents the effect. Our argument concerns a part that keeps the same nature as the whole, with no new condition added. A part may change when separated from the whole. If it does not change, then each part has an effect that is a part of the whole effect, even if it can act only when joined to the others. If it did change when the parts came together, then something new would have been added. The parts would be parts of the material from which the force is made, not parts of the force itself.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00683

Think again of ten people carrying a heavy load. When they act together, each carries a share of it. When one stands alone, the way the load and the other people support it may change. Even then, each person could contribute an effect to the receiver if the receiver remained in a condition where the effects could be added. When the tenth person's share is added to the other nine, the load is lifted just as before. If the workers separate, opposing forces may prevent the load from moving. A small fire may also fail to burn because the stone's opposite nature overcomes it. Without such obstacles, the fire's effect would match its strength.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00684
We cannot overturn a general proof with particular examples when we do not know all the details of the cause and the thing being affected.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00685

A third objection says the philosophers agree that we cannot compare things that do not exist as greater or smaller. They used this principle to answer an argument that time had a beginning. Why, then, do they compare what a bodily force can affect, even when those effects do not exist? They seem to be like numbers that have not yet been counted.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00686

I reply that effects a force can bring about may not exist in separate detail, but they do exist together within the force, as a possibility built into it. The connection between things and the source that produces them is strong. A part of a force has, by its nature, some power to produce an effect; the whole force has the same kind of power. So it makes sense to say that what the part can do is less than what the whole can do, even if neither effect has yet occurred. The power's ability to produce an effect is already real; the effect itself has one kind of existence within that power and another when it is actually produced. In making this comparison, we are considering what the power is capable of, not what has already happened. If the part's capacity is only part of the whole capacity, then the whole capacity is finite. And if it is finite, what it can affect is finite too, whether that exists in fact or only within the power.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00687
A fourth objection says that if the earth stayed forever in its place, and nothing interfered with it, its power would produce one lasting effect: permanent rest.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00688

I reply that one and the same natural body cannot remain forever in one place, in one action, or in one state. This helps us see that no body remains forever, whether on its own or because other principles continue to support it. Whatever belongs to a thing does so through its existence. So if a force cannot produce an unlimited effect by itself, it cannot do so through something else either.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00689

Avicenna's reply in The Discussions is that rest is an absence, not an action, and is not divided by time. The time of rest comes from another power, the one that causes motion. The earth's power does not produce an action by resting. If there is an unlimited action, it comes from another power that produces unlimited time, and so makes rest unlimited.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00690

Someone might reply that even if rest is an absence, the earth's being in its place belongs to the category of place and is an attribute. Its color, shape, weight, size, matter, and all its other qualities are also attributes, some of quality, some of quantity, and some of substance, as with its bodily nature. In some way, all of these are caused by the earth's nature and come from it, as we have already said.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00691

A fifth objection appeals to the orbits of the heavens. They differ in number without limit. The power moving the moon's sphere can make more revolutions than the power moving Saturn's sphere. So the two powers are finite, and the motions they produce should be finite as well. But if the motions do not have to be finite just because the powers differ in their effects, then the same should be true of the effects of a whole power and one of its parts.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00692

We reply that the powers moving the moon and Saturn differ in their nature and kind, not as whole and part. That puts them outside the question we are discussing. We have shown that when one power is part of another, its capacity must be part of the whole capacity. Both capacities must therefore be finite, since their only difference is in size. But the powers moving the heavens are different kinds of power, and their motions are different kinds of motion. One power's action is not a part of another's, and cannot be measured as larger or smaller. A straight line and a circle, for example, have no ratio of length or number between them. Our point is not that the actual effects of a whole and a part differ. It is that their capacities differ. So no one can say the moon makes more revolutions than Saturn in the sense needed here. We cannot compare effects that do not yet exist as more or less. Nor can we say that one heavenly power has more capacity than another, since neither is part of the other.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00693

A sixth objection appeals to the souls of the heavens. They are bodily powers, yet they produce unlimited acts of will and motion. The reply that an intellect moves the heavens is weak. If an intellectual power moves them, it either produces motion by itself, or gives the body a power by which it moves. If it gives the body a bodily power, then a bodily power produces unlimited actions. But if the intellectual power directly produces motion, the bodily power is not the source of that motion, contrary to what we established earlier: the immediate cause of motion must undergo some change, while a separate, immaterial cause does not.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00694

Also, bodies share in bodily nature, but some receive the effects of separate causes only because they have a bodily power within them. So the mover must be a bodily power. Some reply that the separate substance produces these motions, using the heavenly souls as intermediaries. The proof, they say, concerns what produces the motions, not the intermediaries.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00695

I say that this reply does not hold. If a bodily power can last for an unlimited time and serve as an intermediary through which a separate cause produces unlimited actions, then a bodily power can be the source of unlimited actions. The intermediary either really shares in the effect or gives the effect to what depends on it. In either case, the intermediary is involved in the unlimited actions. Al-Rāzī makes the point well. If those who say that bodily powers are not effective but only prepare a thing mean that bodily powers cannot be the direct cause of unlimited effects, then there is no need for a separate argument: they already claim bodily powers cannot directly cause any effects, even finite ones. If they mean that bodily powers cannot act as intermediaries between a separate intellect and unlimited effects, that is disproved by the case of the heavenly soul. Why, then, do they allow a bodily power to serve as an intermediary forever here, after denying that it can do so elsewhere?
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00696

Al-Rāzī is right in this discussion, and there is no answer unless we return to our account of how bodily powers renew themselves. A soul that is joined to a body changes and passes away as nature does. But when it knows and is known, it is like the Active Intellect, once it has become intellect in action and has left behind every ability that exists only as a possibility. The truth is that all natures are renewed in their existence and identity. They also move toward God through an inward, meaningful movement, because God is their highest aim. When they reach the level of intellect, they join the divine world and come to rest: they pass away from themselves and remain through God. All bodies and bodily beings—whether natures or souls—are changing, created, and passing away. Everything else remains through God, the One who overcomes all. I will explain this later, if God wills.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00697

The seventh objection says that either a bodily power must reach a time when its own nature makes it impossible for it to exist, or it does not. The first would mean that a thing's nature changes from possible to impossible, which cannot happen. If the agent, the receiver, and the conditions can all last forever, how can the power be unable to last forever? And if the power lasts, it will act. So a power that acts without limit over time is not impossible.
Stage Eight: Further Properties and Rules of Motion
passage-en-00698

I reply that necessity, possibility, and impossibility concern what a thing is in relation to existence in general. The nature of bodily power may allow it to exist and continue. This does not mean that one particular instance of that power can last forever, given its limited existence and the traces of absence and decay within it. Some say that a bodily power must end, not because of its own nature, but because outside forces eventually strike it and destroy it. A power might not need to end in itself, but general causes and the collisions of their particular effects could make its end necessary. This answer is no good. Many things cannot last forever even if we imagine removing every outside force. Every possible thing has some way of existing that cannot last by its own nature.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority

I. What Do “Coming-to-Be” and “Eternity” Mean?
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00701

Coming-to-be and eternity can be understood in two ways. The first compares one thing with another. For example, less time may have passed since Zayd began to exist than since Amr did. In ordinary speech, we call Amr older and Zayd more recent. Eternity and coming-to-be in this sense are relative to one another.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00702

The second way does not compare one thing with another. It has two kinds: temporal and essential. Temporal coming-to-be means that something exists after it did not exist, with its earlier nonexistence and later existence separated in time. In other words, it did not exist at an earlier time. Under this definition, time itself cannot have come into being. We could only imagine its coming-to-be if time had continued while time itself was absent. That would mean time existed at the very point when we suppose it did not, which is impossible. That is why Aristotle, the First Teacher of the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, said that anyone who says time came into being has, without realizing it, also said that it is eternal.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00703

As you will learn in the discussion of time, time itself is what we describe as earlier and later. These are features of what time is, even before we consider its existence. Each part of time is “before,” when compared with what follows it, and “after,” when compared with what came before it. So time does not begin after a period of nonexistence. Yet change and renewal belong to time and motion by their very nature. In the world, time is not something added to motion. It is distinct from motion only in thought, as something we draw out of the idea of motion. Temporal eternity means that the time during which something exists has no beginning. Time itself is not eternal in this sense, because there is no other time in which it could exist.
Stage Nine: Eternity, Coming-to-Be, and the Kinds of Priority and Posteriority
passage-en-00704

Things that are entirely separate from matter also do not exist in time, since they are above time. The author of Al-Muṭāraḥāt was therefore wrong to say that, under every accepted meaning, nothing falls outside the categories of eternity and coming-to-be. You will see that nothing in existence is eternal in the temporal sense. The second kind is not temporal. It is called essential coming-to-be or essential eternity. Essential coming-to-be means that a thing's existence does not rest on itself but depends on something else. This dependence may be limited to a certain time, may continue at every time, or may lie beyond time and motion. This is essential coming-to-be.
